title: Organs inside you: where they sit and what they do

summary.text: Most people think the stomach is behind the belly button, but it sits higher, under the ribs on the left. An organ is a body part with a special job. Your heart pumps blood, your lungs take in air, your stomach churns food and your brain sends and receives messages. Bone and liquid protect the soft organs, and each organ needs all the others to stay alive. Scientists know where organs are and what they do, but not yet how a brain makes a thought.
summary.art: A friendly see-through outline of a child, showing a pink brain in the head, two spongy lungs and a red fist-sized heart in the chest, and a J-shaped stomach under the left ribs.

intro.hook: Put your hand flat on your chest and keep very still. You can feel a beat under your hand. It started before you were born, and it goes on while you sleep. What is beating, and where exactly is it?
intro.text: Your heart, lungs, stomach and brain are hidden under your skin and bones. You cannot see them, but you can feel what they do. You can feel a beat in your chest, air filling you up and a full feeling after dinner. In this unit you find out where each organ sits, what it does and how the organs help each other.
intro.art: A child with one hand on the chest and eyes closed, with a dotted outline of a heart glowing faintly under the hand.

outcomes: I can say what an organ is: a body part with a special job, made of many living cells.
I can point to where my heart, lungs, stomach and brain are, on my own body and on a drawing.
I can say the main job of the heart, the lungs, the stomach and the brain in one sentence each.
I can explain how the skull and the ribs protect the organs inside them.
I can give an example of organs working as a team, like when I run or eat.
I can run a fair test with a model organ, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can say what scientists agree about these organs, and what they still do not know, like how the brain makes thoughts.
I can give surprising examples: one cell that uses oxygen, breaks down food and senses on its own, an octopus with three hearts, and mini-organs grown in labs.

terms.meaning: A body part with a special job. It is made of many tiny living cells working together.
terms.example: Your heart is an organ. Its job is to pump blood.
terms.art: Four simple organ shapes in a row: a brain, a heart, two lungs and a stomach, each with a little label tag.

terms.meaning: A strong muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood all around your body.
terms.example: When you run fast, you can feel your heart thumping in your chest.
terms.art: A red fist-sized heart next to a child's closed fist, the same size.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy organs in your chest. They take in air and pass oxygen into your blood.
terms.example: When you blow up a balloon, the air comes out of your lungs.
terms.art: Two pink spongy lungs shaped like tall leaves, with a windpipe joining them at the top.

terms.meaning: A stretchy bag shaped like a letter J. It holds your food, mixes it with juices and churns it into a soup.
terms.example: After a big plate of rice and dal, your stomach stretches to hold it all.
terms.art: A J-shaped stomach, small and wrinkled when empty, big and smooth when full.

terms.meaning: A soft, wrinkly organ inside your head. It sends and receives messages for the whole body. It helps you think, feel, remember and move.
terms.example: Your brain is working right now, helping you read and understand these words.
terms.art: A pink wrinkly brain inside the outline of a head, with tiny sparks for messages.

terms.meaning: The tiniest living piece of a body. Your body is made of about 30 trillion of them. Each one is far too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Your skin, your blood and your heart are all made of cells.
terms.art: A magnifying glass over a patch of skin, showing a neat pattern of tiny round cells.

terms.meaning: A group of the same kind of cells working together. Different tissues join together to make an organ.
terms.example: Muscle tissue in your heart squeezes. Nerve tissue in your brain carries messages.
terms.art: Small identical bricks forming a wall, labelled with a tiny muscle cell picture.

terms.meaning: The red liquid that flows all over your body through tubes called blood vessels. It carries oxygen and food to every cell, and takes waste away.
terms.example: When you scrape your knee, the red drops are blood.
terms.art: A red river flowing through branching tubes, carrying tiny bubbles and food crumbs.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that nearly every cell in your body needs to stay alive. You cannot see it or smell it.
terms.example: Plants give out oxygen. You breathe it in through your nose.
terms.art: A tree giving out small blue bubbles that float towards a child breathing in.

terms.meaning: A waste gas your cells make. Your blood carries it to your lungs, and you breathe it out.
terms.example: The air you breathe out has much more carbon dioxide in it than the air you breathe in.
terms.art: A child breathing out, with small grey dots in the breath labelled carbon dioxide.

terms.meaning: A thin cord, like a cable, made of the long threads of nerve cells. It carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body.
terms.example: When you touch a hot tawa, nerves carry the message 'hot!' to your brain very fast.
terms.art: A thin glowing thread running from a fingertip up the arm to the brain.

terms.meaning: A thick bundle of nerves that runs from your brain down the middle of your back. It sits safe inside your backbone.
terms.example: Run your finger down the bumps on your back. Your spinal cord is inside those bones.
terms.art: A see-through back showing the knobbly backbone with a glowing cord running down inside it.

terms.meaning: The hard bony case around your brain. It works like a helmet.
terms.example: Knock gently on your head. The hard part you feel is your skull.
terms.art: A skull drawn like a helmet with the brain tucked safely inside.

terms.meaning: The curved bones around your chest. They make a cage that guards your heart and lungs.
terms.example: Press gently on the sides of your chest. The hard curved bars are your ribs.
terms.art: A curved rib cage like a birdcage, with a heart and two lungs safe inside.

terms.meaning: A dome-shaped muscle under your lungs. When it pulls down, air rushes into your lungs.
terms.example: When you hiccup, your diaphragm is giving a sudden little jerk.
terms.art: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle under two lungs, with an arrow showing it moving down.

terms.meaning: The tube that carries food from your mouth down to your stomach. Doctors call it the oesophagus.
terms.example: When you swallow a sip of water, it slides down your food pipe in a few seconds.
terms.art: A tube running from the mouth down the neck and chest to a J-shaped stomach.

terms.meaning: Long coiled tubes after the stomach. They take the useful parts of food into your blood.
terms.example: Most of your 'tummy' below the belly button is intestines, not stomach.
terms.art: A long coiled tube folded neatly under a stomach, like a garden hose in a basket.

terms.meaning: Liquids your body makes to break food down into tiny pieces. The stomach's juice has a strong acid in it.
terms.example: When you smell hot pakoras, your mouth fills with saliva, or spit. Saliva is a digestive juice too.
terms.art: Little droplets falling into a stomach where food pieces are breaking apart.

terms.meaning: A team of organs that work together for one big job.
terms.example: Your mouth, food pipe, stomach and intestines are a team for digesting food.
terms.art: Four organs linked by arrows in a loop, like a relay team passing a baton.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that our eyes cannot see. It passes through the soft parts of the body, but bones block most of it. Doctors use it to take pictures of your inside.
terms.example: If you break your arm, a doctor takes an X-ray to see the bone.
terms.art: A glowing X-ray picture of a hand, with the white bones clearly showing.

explanations.definition: An organ is a body part with a special job. It is made of different tissues, and each tissue is made of many cells of one kind.
explanations.description: Think of a house. Bricks are like cells. A wall of bricks is like a tissue. A whole room, built from walls, a floor and a door, is like an organ. A kitchen is a room with a special job. Your stomach is an organ with a special job. Your body has many organs. This unit looks at four big ones inside you: the heart, the lungs, the stomach and the brain. Your skin is an organ too, and it is the biggest one you have.
examples: The heart is an organ. Its job is pumping blood.
The eye is an organ. Its job is seeing.
The skin is an organ. Its job is to cover and protect you.
explanations.art: A brick, a brick wall and a kitchen room side by side, next to a cell, a strip of muscle and a heart.
explanations.context: This card explains the main word of the whole unit: organ.

explanations.concept: The body map: where the four organs live
explanations.definition: The brain is in your head. The heart and lungs are in your chest, behind the ribs. The stomach is in the upper left of your belly, partly tucked under the lowest ribs.
explanations.description: Start at the top. Your brain fills the inside of your head, behind your eyes and above your ears. Go down your neck into your chest. Here your two lungs fill most of the space, one on each side. Your heart is tucked between them, in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left. Now go down to where your ribs end. Your stomach sits on the left, partly tucked under the lowest ribs. Many people think the stomach is behind the belly button. It is higher than that. Most of the soft belly below it is filled with your intestines.
examples: Put a hand on the middle of your chest. Your heart is just behind your breastbone, the flat bone in the middle.
Breathe in deeply with your hands on your ribs. You can feel your lungs filling and your ribs lifting out.
Press gently just under your left ribs after a big meal. That full feeling is your stomach.
explanations.art: A child's body outline with four organs drawn in place, and dotted arrows from labels to the head, the middle of the chest, both sides of the chest and the upper left belly.
explanations.context: This card shows where the heart, lungs, stomach and brain sit in your body.

explanations.concept: The heart: a pump that never rests
explanations.definition: The heart is a hollow muscle about the size of your fist. It squeezes again and again to pump blood all around the body.
explanations.description: Your heart is a bag of strong muscle with four rooms inside. Each squeeze pushes blood out into tubes that reach every part of you. Blood carries oxygen and food to every cell, and carries waste away. Then the heart relaxes, fills with blood again and squeezes again. In a grown-up, this happens about 70 times every minute. That is about one hundred thousand beats every day. A child's heart beats a little faster. The heart is in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left. That is why you feel the beat most on the left. The heart even has its own tiny timekeeper inside it, which starts each beat. It can keep beating for a while even after it is taken out of a body.
examples: A heart going to a person who needs a new one is kept cold in a box. Once it is joined up and warmed, it can start beating again in the new body.
When you are scared, your heart beats faster. Your brain sends a message to speed it up.
A blue whale's heart is as heavy as two grown-up people. A mouse's heart is smaller than a peanut.
explanations.art: A fist-sized heart in the middle of a chest outline, tipped slightly left, with red arrows showing blood going out to the head, arms and legs.
explanations.context: This card is about the heart: where it is and what it does.

explanations.concept: The lungs: two spongy air bags
explanations.definition: The lungs are two soft, spongy organs in the chest. They bring in oxygen from the air and get rid of carbon dioxide.
explanations.description: You have two lungs, one on each side of your heart. They fill most of your chest, from just above your collarbones to low down inside your ribs. Air comes in through your nose or mouth and goes down your windpipe. The windpipe splits into two tubes, one for each lung. Inside, the tubes branch again and again, like the branches of a tree. At the very ends are hundreds of millions of tiny air bags. Oxygen passes from these bags into the blood. Carbon dioxide passes out of the blood and into the bags, and you breathe it out. Your left lung is a little smaller than your right one. It has a dent in it, to make room for your heart. Lungs cannot pull in air by themselves. A dome-shaped muscle under them, the diaphragm, pulls down to make them fill with air.
examples: When you blow out birthday candles, the air comes from your lungs.
The tiny air bags in your lungs, all spread out flat, would cover a large part of a badminton court.
Lungs are so full of air that a piece of lung floats in water.
explanations.art: Two pink lungs on either side of a heart, the left one with a dent, and a windpipe branching like an upside-down tree.
explanations.context: This card is about the lungs: where they are and what they do.

explanations.concept: The stomach: a stretchy bag that churns
explanations.definition: The stomach is a stretchy, muscly bag at the end of the food pipe. It holds food, mixes it with strong juices and churns it into a thick soup.
explanations.description: When you swallow, food slides down your food pipe into your stomach. Your stomach sits under your ribs on the left side, shaped a bit like the letter J. When it is empty, it is small and wrinkly. When you eat, it stretches. A grown-up's stomach can comfortably hold about one litre of food, like a big water bottle. The stomach walls are made of muscle. They squeeze and churn the food, like hands kneading dough. The stomach also makes a juice with a strong acid in it. The acid helps break down food and kills many germs. Why does the stomach not digest itself? It covers its inside with a thick slimy layer, called mucus, and it keeps replacing its lining. After two to four hours, the soupy food moves on into the intestines.
examples: After a festival feast you feel full and tight under your ribs. That is your stomach stretched wide.
A tummy rumble is mostly gas and liquid being squeezed through your stomach and intestines.
Some people have had their whole stomach removed because of an illness. They can still live, by eating small meals often.
explanations.art: A J-shaped stomach under the left ribs, with arrows showing its walls squeezing and food pieces breaking into soup.
explanations.context: This card is about the stomach: where it is and what it does.

explanations.concept: The brain: the body's message centre
explanations.definition: The brain is a soft organ inside the skull. It receives messages from the body, sends messages back and lets us think, feel, remember and move.
explanations.description: Your brain sits inside your skull, floating in a clear liquid that cushions it. In a grown-up it weighs about 1.3 kilograms, a little more than a 1-kilogram packet of atta. It is made of about 86 billion nerve cells, joined in a huge web. Messages race along nerves between the brain and every part of your body. Your eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin send messages in. Your brain sends messages out to your muscles. Some parts of your brain work without you thinking at all. They keep you breathing and change how fast your heart beats, even while you sleep. The brain uses about a fifth of your body's energy, even though it is a small part of your weight. The brain itself cannot feel pain. That is why doctors can sometimes operate on a brain while the person is awake.
examples: When a cricket ball flies towards you, your eyes tell your brain and your brain tells your hands to catch it.
When you sleep, your brain keeps you breathing and sorts out what you learned that day.
Messages cross over. The left side of your brain moves the right side of your body.
explanations.art: A brain inside a head outline, with glowing threads running down the spinal cord to the hands and feet, and little message sparks moving both ways.
explanations.context: This card is about the brain: where it is and what it does.

explanations.concept: Bones that guard the soft organs
explanations.definition: The skull is a hard case around the brain. The rib cage is a cage of curved bones around the heart and lungs.
explanations.description: Your brain, heart and lungs are soft and very important. A hard knock could hurt them. So your body keeps them inside bone. The skull is like a helmet. Inside it, the brain floats in a clear liquid, so it does not bang against the bone when you jump. Your ribs curve round from your backbone to the front of your chest, like the bars of a birdcage. They protect your heart and lungs. But the ribs are not a solid box. They are joined by muscles, and they swing up and out every time you breathe in. This gives your lungs room to get bigger. Your stomach sits partly under the bottom ribs, so it is partly guarded too.
examples: A cricket helmet protects your skull, which protects your brain. That is two helmets.
When you breathe in deeply, your ribs swing up and out, like the handle of a bucket being lifted.
A coconut has a hard shell and liquid inside, a bit like your skull and the liquid around your brain.
explanations.art: A skull drawn as a helmet around a brain, and a rib cage drawn as a birdcage around a heart and two lungs.
explanations.context: This card is about how bones protect the organs inside you.

explanations.definition: Every organ needs the others. The body only works because organs pass things and messages to each other all the time.
explanations.description: Follow a breath and a bite. Your lungs take oxygen from the air. Your stomach and intestines take food from your plate. Your blood picks up both. Your heart pumps that blood to every cell, including the cells of the lungs, the stomach and the heart itself. Your brain keeps watch over all of it. When you run, your brain tells your heart to beat faster and your lungs to breathe faster. When you have just eaten, more blood goes to your stomach. If one organ stops, the others soon have trouble. Even the brain needs the heart's blood every second.
examples: Running for the school bus: the brain speeds up the heart and breathing, so the leg muscles get more oxygen.
After a big lunch, more blood flows to your stomach and intestines, to carry away the food they take in.
If the heart stops for even a few minutes, the brain is badly hurt, because no fresh blood reaches it.
explanations.art: Four organs joined in a ring by arrows: lungs passing oxygen, stomach passing food, heart pushing blood, brain sending message sparks to all of them.
explanations.context: This card is about how the heart, lungs, stomach and brain help each other.

explanations.concept: Zoom in: every cell does a little of every job
explanations.definition: Organs are made of cells. Almost every cell uses oxygen, breaks down food and sends and receives signals, in a tiny way of its own.
explanations.description: Look at a cell in your toe. It is far from your lungs, but it uses oxygen. Tiny parts inside it, called mitochondria, use oxygen and food to make energy. They give out carbon dioxide, which the blood carries back to the lungs. The cell also has tiny bags of strong juice that break down food and worn-out parts, a little like a tiny stomach. And it has sensors on its outside that notice chemicals and pass on signals. Organs are what happens when huge numbers of cells share out the work. Heart cells are very good at squeezing. Nerve cells are very good at carrying messages. But almost every cell still uses oxygen, breaks down food and senses in its own small way. The first living things, long ago, were single cells, and each one did every job by itself.
examples: A single amoeba in pond water has no stomach. It wraps itself around food and breaks it down inside a little bubble.
Heart muscle cells grown in a dish in a lab start to twitch and beat by themselves.
A bacterium has no brain, but it can sense food and swim towards it.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle on a toe showing one cell, with a bean-shaped mitochondrion and a small bubble of juice inside it, and tiny sensors on its outside.
explanations.context: This card zooms in from organs to cells, the tiny living pieces organs are made of.

explanations.concept: Does the gut have a mind of its own?
explanations.description: Your stomach and intestines are wrapped in a net of about 500 million nerve cells. This net can run the squeezing of the gut by itself, even if the nerves to the brain are cut. Some scientists call it the 'second brain'. The gut also sends many messages up to the brain. Scientists are now studying how the gut, and the germs that live in it, may affect our feelings. But how much it matters is still argued about.
examples: People talk about 'butterflies in the tummy' when they are nervous. The brain and the gut are talking to each other.
In tests, the gut of an animal kept squeezing food along even after it had been cut off from the brain.
Most of the body's serotonin, a chemical the brain also uses for mood, is made in the gut.

perspectives.who: Michael Gershon, a scientist who wrote a book called The Second Brain in 1998
perspectives.explanation: The gut's nerve net is so big and so independent that it is fair to call it a second brain. It makes its own decisions about digesting food.
The gut's nerve net runs digestion very well. But it is much smaller and simpler than the brain, so calling it a brain can confuse people.
The trillions of germs in our gut seem to send signals that reach the brain. In mice, they change behaviour. Whether they change human feelings much is still being tested.

explanations.art: A stomach and coiled intestines covered in a fine glowing net of nerves, with a dotted line of messages running up to the brain.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: how much the stomach and gut decide on their own.

explanations.description: Scientists agree the brain is needed for thinking and feeling. If part of the brain is hurt, a person can lose words or memories, or even feel differently. But nobody knows how a lump of nerve cells makes the feeling of being you. People have argued about this for thousands of years. Here are the main ideas.
examples: People with an artificial heart pump still think, love and laugh as before. That shows the heart is not where thinking happens.
When you dream, your brain makes a whole world that is not really there.
Brain scans show different parts of the brain lighting up when you read, sing or feel scared.

perspectives.explanation: The mind is what the brain does, the way digestion is what the stomach does. When we understand the brain fully, we will understand the mind.
We can explain how the brain sorts messages. But it is much harder to explain why it feels like anything at all to be you. He called this the 'hard problem'.

perspectives.who: The Upanishads and many sages of India
perspectives.explanation: Awareness is not made by the body. The body, brain and mind appear in awareness, the way waves appear in the sea.

explanations.art: A child looking into a mirror, with the reflection showing a glowing brain and a question mark floating where the child's thoughts would be.
explanations.context: This card is about a big open question: is your brain the same as your mind?

explanations.definition: Most animals have organs for pumping, breathing, digesting and sensing, but they come in many shapes and numbers.
explanations.description: An octopus has three hearts. Two pump blood through its gills and one pumps blood round its body. It also has a brain, and most of its nerve cells are in its eight arms. A cow's stomach has four parts. It brings grass back up to chew again, which is called chewing the cud. A fish has no lungs. It breathes with gills. But many fish have an air bag inside called a swim bladder, and scientists have found that lungs and swim bladders come from the same ancient beginning. A starfish can push its stomach out of its mouth to digest a mussel outside its body. And a sponge, one of the oldest kinds of animals, has no organs at all. Every cell does its own breathing and eating.
examples: Cows and buffaloes chewing slowly while resting are chewing the cud.
An earthworm has five pairs of pumping tubes near its front end, often called its five hearts.
A jellyfish has no brain. It has a net of nerves spread all through its body.
explanations.art: Four small panels: an octopus with three hearts glowing, a cow with a four-part stomach, a fish with gills and a swim bladder, a sponge full of holes.
explanations.context: This card compares our organs with the organs of other animals.

explanations.concept: How we found out what is inside
explanations.definition: People learned about organs by looking carefully inside bodies, by testing ideas, and later by using X-rays and scanners.
explanations.description: For thousands of years, nobody could see inside a living body. The ancient Egyptians, when they made mummies, took out the brain and threw it away, but kept the heart in the body. They thought the heart was where a person's thinking lived. The Greek thinker Aristotle thought so too. About 2,300 years ago, Herophilus, a Greek doctor in Alexandria, cut open human bodies and traced the nerves back to the brain. About 450 years later, the Greek doctor Galen, working in Rome, cut nerves in living animals and showed that the brain controls the voice and movement. In India, the Sushruta Samhita, an old book of surgery, told students to soak a body in a stream for seven days, then gently brush away the skin and flesh layer by layer. In 1543, Andreas Vesalius printed careful drawings of the inside of the human body, and fixed many old mistakes. In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays, and for the first time doctors could see bones inside a living person. Today, scanners like ultrasound and MRI let doctors see a beating heart and a working brain, without any cutting.
examples: A pregnant mother can see her baby's beating heart on an ultrasound screen.
The very first X-ray of a hand was of the hand of Röntgen's wife, Anna Bertha, wearing her ring.
Doctors use X-rays to find a swallowed coin or marble inside a child.
explanations.art: A timeline strip: an Egyptian jar for a mummy's organs, an old printed anatomy drawing, an X-ray of a hand with a ring, and a modern scanner screen showing a heart.
explanations.context: This card tells how people found out what is inside the body.

explanations.description: Scientists can now grow tiny bits of organs in a dish, from a person's own cells. They are called organoids. In 2013, Madeline Lancaster, working in Jürgen Knoblich's lab in Vienna, grew tiny 'mini-brains' the size of a lentil. Others have grown mini-stomachs and mini-guts. These help scientists test medicines and understand illnesses. Nobody can yet grow a full working heart, lung, stomach or brain to put into a person. Scientists hope this may happen one day, but nobody knows when.
examples: Mini-guts grown from a sick child's cells can be used to test which medicine works best for that child.
Scientists have built machines that pump blood for people waiting for a new heart.
Mini-brains in a dish are far too small and simple to work like a whole brain.
explanations.art: A small round lab dish holding a few tiny pink blobs, with a scientist looking at them through a microscope.
explanations.context: This card is about something scientists are just beginning to do: growing tiny organs in a lab.

agreed.text: The heart is in the middle of the chest, tipped a little to the left, and it pumps blood around the body.
agreed.evidence: Doctors can see it beating with ultrasound. In 1628, William Harvey measured how much blood the heart pushes out and showed that blood goes round and round.

agreed.text: The lungs take oxygen from the air into the blood and send carbon dioxide out.
agreed.evidence: The air you breathe out has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air you breathe in. Scientists have measured this many times.

agreed.text: The stomach holds food and breaks it down with churning muscles and strong juices.
agreed.evidence: In the 1820s, a doctor called William Beaumont watched digestion through a hole that a gunshot left in a man's stomach. Today, doctors look inside with a tiny camera on a tube.

agreed.text: The brain controls the body and is needed for thinking, feeling and remembering.
agreed.evidence: When a part of the brain is hurt, the job of that part changes or stops. Scanners show parts of the brain becoming busy during different tasks.

agreed.text: Organs are made of cells, and every organ depends on the others.
agreed.evidence: Microscopes show cells in every organ. When one organ fails, doctors see other organs struggle too.

challenging.claim: We think with our heart, not our brain.
challenging.who: The ancient Egyptians, and the Greek thinker Aristotle about 2,350 years ago. We still say 'learn by heart'.
challenging.for: Your heart races when you are scared, excited or in love. It is warm and always moving. A brain looks like a grey, still lump.
challenging.against: People with an artificial heart pump think and feel as before. When the brain is hurt, thinking changes. The heart races because the brain tells it to.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where thinking happens, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: We only use ten per cent of our brain.
challenging.who: A popular saying, found in films and adverts
challenging.for: It sounds exciting. It suggests we have hidden powers waiting to be switched on.
challenging.against: Brain scans show that over a day almost every part of the brain is busy. Damage to any part causes problems. The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy, and a body would waste that feeding parts it never used.
challenging.context: This card is about a common myth about the brain.

challenging.claim: Stomach ulcers, sore patches in the stomach, are caused by stress and spicy food.
challenging.for: Many people with ulcers were worried and busy. Spicy food can make a sore stomach feel worse.
challenging.against: In Australia, Robin Warren found a germ in the stomachs of people with ulcers. Barry Marshall then drank a cup of these germs to prove it, and his stomach became sore and swollen inside. Medicines that kill the germ cure most ulcers. They won the Nobel Prize in 2005.
challenging.context: This card is about a medical idea that turned out to be wrong, and the scientist who proved it.

challenging.claim: The heart is on the left side of the chest.
challenging.who: What most of us learn, from putting a hand on our heart
challenging.for: You feel the beat most strongly on the left.
challenging.against: The heart is in the middle of the chest, behind the breastbone, with about two-thirds of it left of the middle. Its pointy bottom tips to the left, and that is where the beat feels strongest.
challenging.context: This card is about where the heart really sits.

challenging.claim: The brain is the boss of all the organs.
challenging.who: A common way of describing the body
challenging.for: The brain sends messages that speed up the heart, change breathing and control muscles.
challenging.against: The heart starts each beat by itself. The gut can run its own squeezing. And the brain dies within minutes without the heart's blood. Some scientists say the body is more like a team than a kingdom.
challenging.context: This card is about whether one organ is really in charge.

challenging.claim: We have found all the organs in the body.
challenging.for: People have studied bodies closely for hundreds of years.
challenging.against: In 2016, a surgeon called J. Calvin Coffey argued the mesentery, a folded sheet holding the intestines, should count as one organ. In 2018, scientists argued that a web of fluid-filled spaces, the interstitium, could be one too. Others say these are new names, not new organs.
challenging.context: This card is about an argument over what counts as an organ.

big_questions.q: Your heart has been beating since before you were born. Who is making it beat? Is it you?
big_questions.hint: Can you stop your heart just by deciding to? Can you hold your breath? What is the difference?

big_questions.q: Your brain is inside a dark, quiet skull. It never sees light. So how do you see colours?
big_questions.hint: Your eyes send messages along nerves. What is the brain doing with those messages?

big_questions.q: If every cell in your toe uses oxygen, why do we need lungs at all?
big_questions.hint: How far is your toe from the air outside? How would oxygen get there by itself?

big_questions.q: The stomach makes acid strong enough to break down meat. Why does it not break down itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about the slimy layer inside, and how fast the stomach replaces its lining.

big_questions.q: Is your brain you? Or is it something you have, like your hands?
big_questions.hint: Who is it that says 'my brain'?

big_questions.q: A heart from one person can keep another person alive. Is it still the first person's heart?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a heart is made of, and whose blood it pumps now.

big_questions.q: In India, many people wait years for a new heart, lung or kidney. Is it fair? Who should get one first?
big_questions.hint: Should it be who waited longest, who is most ill, or who is youngest? Why?

big_questions.q: Your brain floats in a liquid inside your skull. Why is a hard skull alone not enough to keep it safe?
big_questions.hint: Remember the egg test: something soft in an empty jar, and something soft in a jar full of water.

big_questions.q: A sponge has no organs, but it is alive. What is the smallest thing that can still be alive?

big_questions.q: People used to think the heart did the thinking. Which of our ideas today might turn out to be wrong?

story.title: The Marble and the Pomfret
story.note: Meenu, Appu, Amma and the doctor are made up. The facts are real: X-rays show glass and bones, the stomach sits under the left ribs, a fish's heart sits low behind its gills, and lungs and the swim bladders of fish come from the same ancient beginning. Small smooth swallowed things usually pass through safely, but a child who swallows anything must always see a doctor. On an X-ray the lungs look dark, because air lets X-rays through, and the heart looks paler.
text: Meenu did not like insides. She liked outsides. She liked the shine on a fish's skin, the blue on a crab's claw, the pink of a sunset over the Versova boats. Insides were dark and squishy and secret. When Amma cleaned fish on the back step, Meenu looked at the sky.
"You eat fish," said Amma, her knife quick and sure. "You can look at fish."
"I can eat without looking," said Meenu.

Amma laughed and laid a silver pomfret flat on the board. "Then just listen. Here, low down behind the gills, is its heart. Small as a bean. Here is its stomach, a little bag, with the gut curling on after it. Up here, inside the head, in its own bony box, is its brain. And here," she lifted something thin and shiny, like a balloon with the air let out, "is its air bag. It fills this to float."
"Fish don't have lungs," said Meenu, not looking.
"No," said Amma. "But this is a cousin of lungs, from long, long ago. Your teacher can tell you."
Meenu did not ask her teacher. She did not want to think about it.

That night her little brother Appu was playing with his marbles on the floor. Appu was four. He liked to hold things in his mouth, the way a dog holds a stick. Meenu was doing sums. She heard a small click, then a gulp, then nothing at all.
Appu was looking at her with very round eyes. One marble was missing. The green one, with the twist of white inside, like a little galaxy.
"Appu," said Meenu, "where is the green one?"
Appu pointed at his mouth. Then he pointed at his belly button. Then he began to cry.

Everything after that was fast. Amma's hands on Appu's cheeks. "Can you breathe? Breathe for me." Appu breathing, loud and wet and angry. Baba running for an auto. Meenu squeezed in at the back, holding Appu's foot, because it was the only part of him she could reach.
In the auto, Appu cried, "It's in my tummy! It will stay in my tummy for ever!" He pressed his belly button as if he could push the marble back up.
Meenu thought of the insides of him. Dark and squishy and secret. Where did a marble even go, in there? Was it lost? Could a person get lost inside themselves?

At the hospital, a doctor with tired eyes and a kind voice listened to Appu's chest. "His breathing is clear," she told Amma. "That means the marble went down the food pipe, not the windpipe. Good. Now let us see where it is."
They took Appu into a room with a big grey machine. They let Meenu stand behind a glass window with Amma. There was a buzz. Then a picture lit up on a screen.
It was Appu. But it was Appu from the inside.

Meenu stared. She saw the round white bowl of his skull. She saw a long chain of white beads running down the middle of him, his backbone. And she saw curved white bars, row after row, wrapping round his chest.
"Ribs," Meenu whispered. "Like the pomfret's bones."
In the dark space inside the ribs there were two big dark patches, one on each side. Between them was a paler shape, tipped a little to the left.
"Lungs," said the doctor, pointing. "And his heart, in the middle. Do you see how they fit together? The left lung is a bit smaller, to leave room for the heart."
And there, just below the ribs, a little to the left, was a small, perfect white circle. A tiny full moon.
"The marble," said the doctor. "Glass shows up white, like bone. It is sitting in his stomach."
"Not his tummy?" said Meenu. She had thought the stomach was behind the belly button, where Appu had pointed.
"The stomach is higher than most people think," said the doctor. "Under the ribs, on the left. Shaped a little like a J. After the stomach come the long, curly intestines. That is most of the tummy."
Meenu looked at the white moon under the ribs. A little bag, with the gut curling on after it. She had heard those words before, on the back step, in Amma's voice.
"It's the same," she said slowly. "It's the same as the fish."
The doctor raised her eyebrows. Amma smiled a small, surprised smile.

"A brain in its own bony box, at the top," said Meenu. "A heart near the front. A stomach after the food pipe, and the gut after that. Only the fish has an air bag, and Appu has lungs." She remembered the thin shiny balloon. "Cousins," she said.
"That is right," said the doctor. "Very long ago, they began as the same thing."

The doctor told Amma what would happen next. A small, smooth marble almost always travels on by itself, she said. It moves from the stomach into the intestines, slowly, slowly, along the whole long journey, and comes out at the end. They must watch Appu, and come straight back if his tummy hurt or he was sick.
On the auto ride home, Appu was sleepy and hiccuping. "Is it lost?" he asked.

Meenu put her hand gently on him, just below his ribs, on the left. "No," she said. "It's here. In your stomach. Your stomach is squeezing it, like Amma kneading dough. Tomorrow it goes into the long curly tube. Then it goes all the way along, and then out."
"How do you know?" said Appu.
"I saw the map," said Meenu. "Inside you there is a map. It's the same map as the fish."
Appu thought about that. Then he put his own small hand on top of hers, and they rode like that, through the orange streetlights, past the dark sea.

Two days later, the green marble came out, exactly the way the doctor had said. Baba washed it in hot soapy water three times, and then three times again, and then everyone laughed so much that Appu got hiccups again.
The next Sunday, Amma laid a pomfret on the board. Meenu sat down on the step beside her. She did not look at the sky.
"Show me the heart," she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenu is frightened of 'insides' because they seem dark, unmapped and secret. The turn comes when the X-ray shows that the inside has a plan: a brain in a bony box at the top, a heart in the middle inside a cage of ribs, lungs on either side, and a stomach under the left ribs, not behind the belly button. Knowing where an organ is turns fear into understanding. Underneath, she sees that the fish and her brother are built on the same plan, because all animals with backbones share an ancestor. Lungs and a fish's swim bladder began as one thing.
ask: Where did Appu point when he said the marble was in his tummy? Where was it really?
How did the doctor know the marble had not gone into Appu's windpipe?
What did Meenu see on the X-ray that reminded her of the fish?
Why was Meenu afraid of insides at the start? Why do you think she was not afraid at the end?
Meenu said, 'Inside you there is a map.' What would your map show?
Is there something you are a bit scared of because you do not know much about it yet?

games.title: Where Am I? The Organ Clue Game
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a clue card game about the organs inside you. A player reads a clue, and everyone races to put the right organ token in the right place on a body board.

printables.title: A body outline board, about A3 size
items: An outline of a child's body, front view, with the skull, rib cage and backbone drawn lightly in grey, and no organs drawn in.

printables.title: Organ tokens to cut out, one set per player
24 clue cards to cut out
items: I sit inside a bony helmet. Who am I?
I am about the size of your fist. I squeeze all day and all night. Who am I?
There are two of us. We are soft and spongy, and we are full of air. Who are we?
I am shaped like a J. I sit under your ribs on the left. Who am I?
I float in a clear liquid that stops me banging on bone. Who am I?
I am smaller than my twin, because I leave room for the heart. Who am I?
I am a stretchy bag. I make a strong acid. Who am I?
I am a long, coiled tube. Most of your tummy below the belly button is me. Who am I?
I carry food from your mouth down to the stomach. Who am I?
I carry air from your nose down to the lungs. Who am I?
I have about 86 billion nerve cells. Who am I?
I sit in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left. Who am I?
I keep you breathing even when you are fast asleep. Who am I?
I churn your food like hands kneading dough. Who am I?
I have four chambers, or rooms, inside me, and blood flows through them. Who am I?
Oxygen passes through my hundreds of millions of tiny air bags into your blood. Who am I?
TEAM CARD: You are running for the bus. Point to the two organs that speed up.
TEAM CARD: You just ate a big lunch. Point to the organ that is stretched wide.
TEAM CARD: You are doing a hard puzzle. Which organ is using a lot of energy?
TEAM CARD: You hold your breath. Which organ is telling you to breathe again?
FEEL IT: Everyone puts a hand on the middle of their chest. What can you feel?
FEEL IT: Everyone breathes in deeply with hands on their ribs. What moves?
FEEL IT: Everyone knocks gently on their head. What is the hard part called?
FEEL IT: Everyone swallows a sip of water. Where does it go?

rules: Lay the body board in the middle. Give each player a set of organ tokens.
Shuffle the clue cards and put them face down.
One player reads the top card out loud.
Everyone races to put the right token in the right place on their own board outline, or points to it on the shared board.
The first player to get both the organ and the place right wins the card.
On a TEAM card, everyone answers together and each right answer wins a card. On a FEEL IT card, everyone does it together, then says what they felt.
When the cards run out, the player with the most cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the body board on the floor. 2. Give each player a set of organ tokens. 3. Shuffle the clue cards and put them face down.
flow.say: This is a game about the organs inside us. An organ is a body part with a special job. I read a clue, and you race to put that organ in the right place.
flow.kid: Lay out the body board. Take your organ tokens. Mix the clue cards. Put them face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Am I?, a clue game about where organs sit in your body. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice card together: 'I am shaped like a J. I sit under your ribs on the left. Who am I?'
flow.say: Practice card. 'I am shaped like a J. I sit under your ribs on the left.' Who am I? And where do I go?
flow.kid: Practice card. A J shape, under the ribs on the left. Who is it? Put it on the board.

check.q: Where does the stomach go on the body board?
options: Under the ribs, on the left
In the middle of the chest
check.why: The stomach sits just under the ribs on the left side, shaped like a J. Many people put it behind the belly button, because we call the whole belly the 'tummy'. But the belly below the belly button is mostly intestines. The middle of the chest is where the heart is.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading cards. 2. Everyone races to place the token. 3. Check the place on the board together before giving the card.
flow.say: Read your card. Everyone race! Then we check together: is that the right organ, in the right place?
flow.kid: Read the clue. Race to place the organ. Check it together. Right organ and right place wins the card.
flow.parent: Common mix-ups: putting the heart far to the left, putting the stomach low behind the belly button, and making the lungs tiny. The lungs fill most of the chest, from just above the collarbones to low down inside the ribs. The heart sits between them in the middle.

flow.do: When a TEAM card comes up, everyone answers together.
flow.say: Team card! 'You are running for the bus. Point to the two organs that speed up.'
flow.kid: Team card. You are running for the bus. Which two organs speed up?

check.q: You are running for the bus. Which two organs speed up?
check.why: Running muscles need lots of oxygen. So the lungs breathe faster to take in more air, and the heart beats faster to carry it. Picking the stomach is a fair guess, because a 'stitch' when running hurts in the side of the belly. But the organs that speed up are the heart and the lungs.

flow.do: Count the cards. Then ask each player to point to all four big organs on their own body.
flow.say: Count your cards! Now, without the board, point to your own brain, heart, lungs and stomach.
flow.kid: Count your cards. Now point to your own brain, heart, lungs and stomach.
flow.think: Which organ was hardest to place? Why do you think so?

games.title: Busy Day: The Body Team Game
games.context: This is a board game about organs working as a team. Each player looks after one organ, and event cards from a busy day tell you which organs must work harder.

items: BRAIN: you send and receive messages

printables.title: 18 event cards from a busy day

Run to catch the school bus
Get a fright when a dog barks
Smell food cooking and feel hungry
Climb the stairs to the roof

rules: Each player takes an organ role card. With fewer than 4 players, some players take two.
Shuffle the event cards and put them face down.
On your turn, turn over an event card and move one square along the day track.
Every player whose organ works harder in that event says why, and takes one energy token.
If a player says why clearly, they get one more token.
The brain player can take a token on most cards, but must say what message the brain sends.
When the day ends at the moon, everyone counts tokens. Then talk: did any organ get through the day alone?

flow.context: This is the first step of Busy Day, a game about how the heart, lungs, stomach and brain work as a team. Here you set up the game.
