flow.say: Practice card: a big breakfast. Which organs work harder?
flow.kid: Practice card: a big breakfast. Who works harder? Say why.

check.q: You eat a big breakfast. Which organ is busiest?
check.why: The stomach stretches to hold the food, and churns it with its juices. The brain also tells the stomach to get ready, even when you just smell the food. The lungs are not much busier at breakfast.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over cards and moving along the track. 2. Players whose organ works harder take a token and say why.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the event. Who works harder? Tell us why.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Move one square. Does your organ work harder? Take a token and say why.
flow.parent: Good answers: running, kabaddi, swimming and stairs make the heart and lungs work harder. Meals make the stomach work harder. Hard sums, reading and dreaming keep the brain busy. A fright makes the brain speed up the heart. Sleep slows the heart and breathing, but the brain stays busy.

flow.do: At the moon, count tokens. Then ask the team question.
flow.say: Let's count. Now the big question. Did any organ get through the whole day alone, without the others?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Did any organ do the day alone?

ask.q: Could the brain do its work without the heart?
good: No. The heart sends it blood with oxygen.
No. Without blood, the brain stops working in minutes.

flow.think: Which event card made all four organs busy at once?

items.p: What is an organ?
opts: A body part with a special job, made of many cells
A kind of musical instrument only
items.why: An organ is a body part with a special job, like the heart pumping blood. It is made of many living cells working together. Picking 'any bone' mixes up organs with the skeleton. Each bone is in fact counted as an organ too, but most organs are soft. Picking 'musical instrument' is a fun mix-up, because the word organ means that too.

items.p: Where is your heart?
opts: On the far left of your chest
In the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left
items.why: The heart sits in the middle of the chest, behind the breastbone, with its pointy end tipped to the left. Picking 'far left' is very common, because the beat feels strongest there.
items.art: A chest outline with a heart in the middle, tipped left.

items.p: What is the main job of the lungs?
opts: To take oxygen from the air into the blood
items.why: The lungs take in air, pass oxygen into the blood and let out carbon dioxide. Picking 'pump blood' mixes them up with the heart, their next-door neighbour.

items.p: Where is your stomach?
opts: Under your ribs, on the left
In the middle of your chest
items.why: The stomach is just under the ribs on the left side. Below the belly button are mostly the intestines. Picking 'belly button' happens because we call the whole belly the 'tummy'.

items.p: Which organ sends and receives messages for the whole body?
items.why: The brain sends and receives messages along nerves to every part of the body. Picking 'the heart' is an old idea. Aristotle thought the heart did the thinking. Today we know it is the brain.

items.p: Your heart is about the size of your ____.
items.why: Make a fist. A heart is about that size. A grown-up's heart is the size of a grown-up's fist.

items.p: The hard bony case that protects your brain is called the ____.
items.why: The skull works like a helmet around the brain.

items.p: The curved bones that guard your heart and lungs are your ____.
items.why: The ribs make a cage around the chest. They are joined by muscles and swing up and out, so the lungs have room to get bigger when you breathe in.

items.p: Match each organ to its job.
items.why: Each organ has a main job. They all need each other to do it.

items.p: Match each organ to where it lives.
items.why: Remember the body map: brain at the top, heart and lungs in the chest, stomach just below the ribs on the left.

items.p: You have two lungs.
items.why: True. One lung is on each side of the heart. The left one is a little smaller.

items.p: Your heart stops beating when you are asleep.
items.why: False. Your heart beats all day and all night, your whole life. It just beats a little more slowly when you sleep.

items.p: In the egg in the jar test, the egg (or banana) in water was safer than the one in the empty jar.
items.why: True. The water filled the jar, so the egg moved with the jar and did not crash into its sides. The liquid around your brain does the same job.

items.p: Sort these into the organ that does them: pumping blood, churning food, breathing in oxygen, remembering a song.
items.why: Each job belongs to one main organ, though all four need each other.

items.p: Label the body outline: brain, heart, left lung, right lung, stomach.
items.a: Brain in the head. Heart in the middle of the chest. One lung on each side of the heart. Stomach under the ribs on the left.
items.why: This is the body map. Check your life-size organ map if you are not sure.
items.art: A blank child body outline with five arrows pointing to the head, the middle of the chest, both sides of the chest and the upper left belly.

items.p: Draw yourself. Draw your heart, lungs, stomach and brain in the right places.
items.a: A body with the brain in the head, a fist-sized heart in the middle of the chest, two big lungs on either side, and a J-shaped stomach under the left ribs.
items.why: Drawing a model helps you remember where things are, even the parts you cannot see.

items.p: Why does your brain need your heart? Use the word blood in your answer.
items.a: My heart pumps blood to my brain. The blood carries oxygen and food. Without it, my brain cannot work.
items.why: Every organ needs the heart's blood. The brain stops working within minutes without it.

items.p: Why is your left lung a little smaller than your right lung?
opts: It has a dent to make room for the heart
items.why: The heart tips to the left, so the left lung has a dent for it. Picking 'still growing' guesses that size means age. Both lungs grow at the same time.

items.p: In the squish bag test, why did the squished biscuit break down faster?
opts: Squishing broke it into smaller pieces and mixed it with water
The biscuit was a different kind
It did not break down faster
items.why: Squeezing breaks food into small bits and mixes it. The stomach's muscle walls do the same. Picking 'different biscuit' would make the test unfair. We used the same biscuit in both bags.

items.p: Why do lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny air bags instead of one big bag?
opts: Tiny bags are easier to grow
Many tiny bags give a huge surface for oxygen to pass into the blood
One big bag would be too heavy
items.why: Remember the lump test: the crushed mishri disappeared much faster, because much more of it touched the water. In the same way, many tiny air bags give a huge surface where air meets blood. Spread out flat, they would cover a large part of a badminton court. Picking 'too heavy' guesses about weight. Lungs are very light, because they are full of air.

items.p: The stomach makes a strong acid. Why does the stomach not digest itself?
opts: It has a thick slimy layer and keeps replacing its lining
The brain switches the acid off
items.why: Mucus, a slimy layer, coats the inside of the stomach, and the lining is replaced again and again. Picking 'the acid is weak' is a common idea. In fact the acid is strong enough to help break down meat.

items.p: When you are scared, your heart beats faster. Which organ tells it to?
items.why: The brain sends messages that speed up the heart when you are scared or running. The heart starts each beat itself, but the brain changes the speed. Picking 'it decides alone' is half right, which is why this is a good thing to think about.

items.p: Put these in order, the way food travels: stomach, mouth, intestines, food pipe.
items.why: Food goes in at the mouth, down the food pipe to the stomach, and then on into the intestines.

items.p: Put these in order, the way air travels: lungs, nose, tiny air bags, windpipe.
items.why: Air goes in at the nose, down the windpipe, into the lungs and right to the tiny air bags at the ends of the branches.

items.p: The brain floats in a clear ____ that cushions it.
items.why: Like the water around the egg in the jar, the liquid stops the brain banging on the skull.

items.p: The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs is called the ____.
items.why: Lungs cannot pull in air by themselves. The diaphragm pulls down to make them fill with air.

items.p: The brain itself cannot feel pain.
items.why: True. The brain has no pain sensors of its own. That is why doctors can sometimes operate on a brain while the person is awake.

items.p: We only use ten per cent of our brain.
items.why: False. Brain scans show almost every part of the brain is busy over a day. This is a popular myth.

items.p: An octopus has three hearts.
items.why: True. Two pump blood through its gills and one pumps it round the body.

items.p: You run to catch the school bus. Say what your brain, heart and lungs each do.
items.a: My brain notices my legs need more oxygen. It tells my heart to beat faster and my lungs to breathe faster. My lungs take in more oxygen. My heart pumps it to my leg muscles.
items.why: This shows organs working as a team. The brain sends messages and the heart and lungs answer.

items.p: In the egg in the jar test, what did the egg stand for? What did the jar stand for? What did the water stand for?
items.a: The egg stood for the brain. The jar stood for the skull. The water stood for the liquid that cushions the brain.
items.why: A model stands for the real thing, so we can test an idea safely.

items.p: Draw the rib cage around a heart and two lungs. Show the gaps between the ribs.
items.a: Curved ribs like the bars of a cage, a heart in the middle, two lungs filling the rest, with small gaps between the ribs.
items.why: The gaps and the moving ribs let the lungs grow bigger when you breathe in.

items.p: A sponge is an animal with no heart, stomach or brain. How does it stay alive?
opts: It does not, it is not really alive
Water flows through it, and its cells take oxygen and food from the water
It only lives for one day
items.why: Water flows through tiny holes in a sponge's body. Each cell takes oxygen straight from the water, and some cells catch bits of food and share them with the others. Organs are what happens when cells share out jobs. Picking 'not really alive' is a common idea, because sponges do not move. But they grow, feed and make baby sponges.

items.p: Heart muscle cells grown in a dish start to beat by themselves. What does this tell us?
opts: The heart needs the brain to start each beat
Heart cells have their own beat built in
items.why: Heart cells beat on their own. The brain only speeds them up or slows them down. Picking 'needs the brain' is the most common idea, and it is only half true.

items.p: Barry Marshall drank a cup of germs in 1984. Why?
opts: To prove a germ causes stomach ulcers
items.why: Doctors did not believe him that a germ caused ulcers. So he tested it on himself, got sick, and showed the germ was there. He and Robin Warren won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Doing this is not safe, and nobody should copy it.

items.p: The ancient Egyptians kept the heart in a mummy but threw away the brain. What did they believe?
opts: The heart was where thinking and feeling lived
They did not know the brain existed
items.why: Like Aristotle, they thought the heart was the centre of the person. Evidence later showed the brain does the thinking. Picking 'did not know it existed' is wrong, because they had to remove it.

items.p: Which of these is an organ the size of two fists, weighing about 1,300 grams in a grown-up?
items.why: A grown-up's brain weighs about 1,300 grams, about two fists in size. The heart is about one fist and 300 grams.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Skull, ribs, brain, backbone.
items.why: The brain is a soft organ. The skull, ribs and backbone are bones that protect soft organs.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Heart, lungs, stomach, gills.
items.why: We have hearts, lungs and stomachs. Gills belong to fish. They are the fish's breathing organs, doing the job our lungs do.

items.p: Some scientists call the gut 'the second brain'. Give one reason for this name, and one reason some scientists do not like it.
items.a: For: the gut has about 500 million nerve cells, and it can run its own squeezing without the brain. Against: the gut's nerve net is much smaller and simpler than the brain, so some scientists say the name confuses people.
items.why: This is a debated idea. A good answer gives both sides.

items.p: Every cell in your toe uses oxygen. So why do you need lungs at all?
items.a: My toe is far from the air. Oxygen cannot reach it by itself. The lungs take oxygen into the blood, and the heart pumps the blood all the way to my toe.
items.why: Big bodies need organs to share out jobs. A tiny sponge cell can get oxygen straight from water.

items.p: Aristotle thought the heart did our thinking. What evidence shows that the brain does?
items.a: People with an artificial heart pump still think and feel. When the brain is hurt, thinking and memory change. Brain scans show the brain busy when we think.
items.why: Scientists change their minds when the evidence is strong. Aristotle had good reasons, but not the evidence we have now.

items.p: Is the brain the boss of the body? Give one reason for yes and one for no.
items.a: Yes: it sends messages that change how fast the heart beats and how fast we breathe. No: the heart starts its own beat, and the brain cannot live for long without the heart's blood.
items.why: This is debated. Some scientists see the body as a team, not a kingdom.

items.p: Scientists have grown full-sized working hearts in a lab and put them into people.
items.why: False. Scientists can grow tiny mini-organs, called organoids. Nobody has yet grown a full working heart for a person.

items.p: A fish's swim bladder and our lungs began, long ago, as the same thing.
items.why: True. Scientists have found that lungs and swim bladders come from the same ancient beginning in early fish.

items.p: The brain has about 86 ____ nerve cells.
items.why: 86 billion is about ten times the number of people on Earth. The Brazilian scientist Suzana Herculano-Houzel counted them in 2009. She turned brains into a soup, then counted the cell centres in a few drops.

items.p: Match each animal to its surprising organ fact.
pairs: pushes its stomach out of its mouth
items.why: Animals solve the same problems, pumping, breathing, digesting and sensing, in many different ways.

items.p: Draw one cell. Inside it, draw a mitochondrion and a small bag of juice. On its outside, draw a few sensors. Write what each one does.
items.a: A round cell with a small bean shape (uses oxygen to make energy), a small bubble (breaks down food and old bits) and little feelers on the outside (sense chemicals).
items.why: Almost every cell does small versions of the jobs that organs do. Organs are teams of cells sharing out jobs.

experiments.title: The Egg in the Jar: how liquid protects the brain
experiments.question: Does liquid around a brain help protect it when you move?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will a raw egg crack first in an empty jar, or in a jar filled to the top with water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two eggs of the same size and two jars of the same size. Shake both the same way, the same number of times. Only the water changes.

materials.item: 2 raw eggs of the same size. No eggs at home? Use 2 pieces of peeled ripe banana, each about as long as your thumb, or 2 cubes of soft tofu.
2 plastic jars with screw lids, the same size, wide enough for an egg and about twice as tall. An old plastic jar for biscuits, peanuts or dry fruit works. A snap-lid takeaway box may leak.
water to fill one jar
a tray or newspaper for spills

experiments.safety: Do this over the sink or a tray. Wash hands with soap after touching raw egg. Use plastic jars, never glass.

schedule.what: Guess, then shake an egg in an empty jar and an egg in a jar full of water. Compare, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two eggs, or the two banana pieces, after the test.
experiments.context: This is the egg in the jar test. A raw egg stands for your soft brain. A jar stands for your skull. You test whether water around the egg protects it, like the liquid around your brain. No eggs? A piece of ripe banana works too.

setup.art: Two clear plastic jars with screw lids side by side, one empty with a raw egg inside, one filled to the top with water and an egg inside.
setup.caption: 1. Put one egg in an empty jar and one egg in a jar full of water.

setup.art: A child's hands shaking a closed plastic jar firmly up and down over a sink.
setup.caption: 2. Shake each jar firmly up and down the same way, 5 times.

setup.art: Two opened jars: the egg from the empty jar cracked, the egg from the water jar whole.
setup.caption: 3. Open them and look closely. Which egg cracked?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to knock gently on their head. 2. Show them the egg and the jars.
flow.say: Knock gently on your head. That hard part is your skull. Your brain is soft, a bit like this raw egg. This jar is like a skull. Inside your skull, your brain floats in a clear liquid. Why do you think it floats?
flow.kid: Knock gently on your head. That is your skull. Your brain inside is soft, like this egg. It floats in liquid. Why?

ask.q: What might the liquid do for the brain?
good: It cushions it.
It stops it banging on the bone.
It keeps it wet.

flow.context: This is the first step of the egg in the jar test, about how your brain is protected inside your skull.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which egg will crack first, and to write down the guess.
flow.say: We will shake an egg in an empty jar and an egg in a jar full of water. Which one do you think will crack? Why? Write your guess.
flow.kid: One egg in an empty jar. One egg in water. Which will crack? Why? Write your guess.

flow.do: 1. Put one egg in the empty jar and screw the lid on. 2. Fill the other jar right to the top with water. Put the egg in, top it up so there is no air, and screw the lid on tight. 3. Over the sink, shake each jar firmly up and down 5 times, the same way. Shake in the air. Do not bang the jar on anything.
flow.say: Same jar, same egg, same shakes. Only the water is different. That keeps the test fair. Five firm shakes, up and down.
flow.kid: Put an egg in each jar. Fill one with water to the top. Close the lids tight. Shake each one firmly up and down, 5 times.
flow.parent: Fill the water jar right to the top, so there is no air gap. An air bubble lets the water slosh, and then the egg can hit the side. If neither egg cracks after 5 shakes, open, look, close and do 5 more, a little harder. Shake both jars the same way each time. Banging a jar on the table can crack even the egg in water, so shake only in the air. With banana or tofu, look for squashed, broken corners instead of cracks.

flow.do: Open both jars over the tray. Look closely at each egg. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Let's look. Is either egg cracked? Look very closely, even for tiny cracks.
flow.kid: Open the jars. Look closely. Is either egg cracked? Write it in the table.

check.q: In the egg in the jar test, which egg is usually safer?
options: The egg in the empty jar
The egg in the jar full of water
check.why: In the empty jar, the egg flies across and hits the hard sides. In the full jar, the water fills all the space. The egg moves along with the water and the jar, so it never crashes into the sides. The liquid around your brain does the same job. Picking 'both are the same' often means thinking only the hard jar protects. The jar helps, but the water protects the egg much better.

flow.do: Talk about where the model is like a real head, and where it is different.
flow.say: Our model is like a head in some ways. How is it different from a real head?
flow.kid: How is the egg like your brain? How is it different?

ask.q: How is a real brain different from the egg?
good: A brain is soft all through, not in a shell.
A real skull fits the brain closely.
A real brain is alive and has blood going to it.

flow.parent: This is why we wear helmets for cycling and cricket. A very big knock can still hurt the brain, even with the liquid.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer for the egg test sounds like this. What I think: liquid around the brain protects it. What I saw: the egg in the empty jar cracked after 10 shakes, and the egg in water did not crack. Why: the water cushions the egg, so it does not bang hard on the jar.

experiments.title: The Squish Bag: does churning help break food down?
experiments.question: Does churning food, like the stomach does, break it down faster?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. After five minutes, will the biscuit in the squished bag or the still bag be more broken up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, put the same biscuit and the same amount of water in each bag, and leave them for the same time. Only the squishing changes.
results_table: What it looks like after 1 minute

materials.item: 2 zip-lock bags, or 2 thin plastic bags closed tightly with a rubber band
2 plain biscuits of the same kind, like Marie or glucose biscuits
water, about 4 tablespoons for each bag
a timer or clock

experiments.safety: Do not eat the mixture. Close the bags tightly before squishing.

schedule.what: Guess, then squish one biscuit bag and leave the other still. Compare after 1 and 5 minutes, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what is inside each bag after 5 minutes.
experiments.context: This is the squish bag test. A plastic bag stands for your stomach. You find out whether squeezing food, the way your stomach walls churn, breaks it down faster.

setup.art: Two zip-lock bags, each with one whole biscuit and a little water, on a table next to a clock.
setup.caption: 1. Put one biscuit and the same water in each bag. Seal them.

setup.art: A child's hands squeezing and kneading one bag while the other bag lies still on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Squish one bag for 5 minutes. Leave the other bag still.

setup.art: The two bags held up side by side: one a smooth brown mush, the other with big soggy lumps.
setup.caption: 3. Hold them up. Which one has fewer lumps?

flow.do: Ask your child to point to where their stomach is. Then show them a zip-lock bag.
flow.say: Point to your stomach. Good, under your ribs on the left. Your stomach is a stretchy bag with muscle walls. The walls squeeze and churn the food. This bag will be our stomach.
flow.kid: Point to your stomach. It is under your ribs, on the left. It squeezes food. This bag will be a stomach.
flow.context: This is the first step of the squish bag test, about how your stomach churns food.

flow.do: 1. Put one biscuit in each bag. 2. Add the same water to each. 3. Squeeze out the air and seal. 4. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Same biscuit, same water. One bag will be squished, one will stay still. Which will be more broken up after five minutes?
flow.kid: Put a biscuit and water in each bag. Seal them. Which will break up more? Guess.

flow.do: 1. Squish one bag gently with your fingers for 5 minutes. 2. Leave the other bag flat and still. 3. After 1 minute, look at both and write in the table. 4. After 5 minutes, look again.
flow.say: Squeeze it like dough. Your stomach does this for hours after a meal. Let's look after one minute. Now keep going.
flow.kid: Squish one bag like dough. Leave the other still. Look after 1 minute. Then after 5 minutes. Write what you see.
flow.parent: Swap hands if they get tired. The still bag will soften a little, because the water soaks in. The squished bag will become a smooth mush much faster.

flow.do: Hold both bags up to the light and compare. Count or guess the lumps.
flow.say: Hold them up to the window. Which has more lumps? Which looks more like soup?
flow.kid: Hold the bags up to the light. Which has more lumps?

check.q: In the squish bag test, which bag usually breaks down more?
check.why: Squishing breaks the biscuit into smaller and smaller bits and mixes it with water. The stomach walls do the same with food. Picking 'the still bag' usually means thinking water alone does all the work. Water helps, but squeezing makes it much faster.

flow.do: Talk about what the bag model leaves out.
flow.say: Our bag only has water. A real stomach adds something else, a strong juice with acid in it. What would that add?
flow.kid: A real stomach also adds a strong juice. What would it do?

ask.q: What does the stomach add that our bag does not?
good: Acid
Digestive juice
Warmth

flow.think: Why do you think grown-ups say to chew your food well?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer for the squish bag test sounds like this. What I think: churning helps the stomach break food down. What I saw: after 5 minutes the squished biscuit was smooth mush, and the still one had big lumps. Why: squeezing breaks food into tiny pieces and mixes it with liquid.

experiments.title: Lump or Bits: why lungs have so many tiny air bags
experiments.question: Does a lump of mishri disappear into water faster whole, or crushed into small bits?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will the whole lump or the crushed lump disappear into the water first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two lumps of mishri the same size, two glasses the same size with the same amount of water from the same jug, and stir both the same way. Only the crushing changes. Do the test twice.

materials.item: 4 lumps of mishri (rock sugar), each about the size of your thumbnail and as alike as you can find. Or 4 sugar cubes.
2 clear glasses the same size, each half full of water from the same jug. Steel tumblers work too, if you look down into them from above.
2 spoons for stirring
a clean cloth and a heavy steel tumbler or rolling pin, for crushing
a clock or a phone timer

experiments.safety: Crush the lump inside a folded cloth, so no bits fly. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Guess, then stir a whole lump of mishri and a crushed one in water, and time how long each takes to disappear. Do it twice. Then talk about the tiny air bags in your lungs.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for the whole lump and a bar for the crushed lump.
experiments.context: This is the lump or bits test. You time how fast sugar disappears into water, whole or crushed. It shows why your lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny air bags instead of one big bag.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until the sugar disappeared
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two lumps of mishri the same size beside two clear glasses half full of water, with a folded cloth and a rolling pin.
setup.caption: 1. Choose two lumps the same size. Crush one inside a cloth.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up each stirring a glass, one with a whole lump and one with crushed sugar, a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Tip each into its own glass. Stir both the same way.

setup.art: Two glasses: one with clear water and no sugar left, the other with a small lump still sitting at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long each takes to disappear.

flow.do: Show your child a lump of mishri. Ask what they notice about its outside.
flow.say: Look at this lump of mishri. Only its outside touches anything around it. Your lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny air bags, not one big bag. Why might that be? Keep your idea in mind.
flow.kid: Look at the mishri lump. Only its outside can touch the water. Your lungs have lots of tiny air bags. Why? Keep your idea.
flow.context: This is the first step of the lump or bits test, about why your lungs have so many tiny air bags.

flow.do: 1. Put one lump inside a folded cloth. 2. Tap it with a heavy steel tumbler or a rolling pin until it is small bits. 3. Ask for a guess, and write it down.
flow.say: This lump is now lots of small bits. Nothing was added or taken away. Which do you think will disappear into the water first, the whole lump or the bits? Why?
flow.kid: Crush one lump inside a cloth. Tap it until it is small bits. Which will disappear first? Why? Write your guess.
flow.parent: Use the same amount of sugar in both. Tip every crushed bit out of the cloth.

flow.do: 1. Tip the whole lump into one glass and the crushed bits into the other, at the same moment. 2. You stir one and your child stirs the other, about one stir each second. 3. Write down how many minutes each takes until you can see no sugar. 4. Do it again with the other two lumps, swapping who stirs which.
flow.say: Ready? Tip them in together. Stir gently, one stir each second. Tell me when you can see no sugar at all. Then we do it again, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Tip both in at the same time. Stir, one stir each second. Watch the clock. When is the sugar gone? Do it twice.
flow.parent: The crushed bits usually vanish in a minute or two. The whole lump takes several minutes, often much longer. If it is still there after 10 minutes, write '10 minutes and still there'. Swapping who stirs keeps the test fair.

flow.do: Draw one bar for the whole lump and one for the crushed lump.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each. Which bar is taller? Which sugar was faster?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for the whole lump and one for the bits. Which is taller?

chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until the sugar disappeared
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In the lump or bits test, why did the crushed sugar disappear faster?
options: It was a different kind of sugar
Much more of the sugar was touching the water
check.why: Crushing did not add any sugar. It made much more of the sugar touch the water at once, so it went into the water faster. Your lungs work the same way. Hundreds of millions of tiny air bags give a huge surface where air meets blood, so a lot of oxygen gets into the blood every second. Picking 'different sugar' or 'hotter water' would make the test unfair. We used the same sugar and the same water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer for the lump test sounds like this. What I think: small bits go into water faster than one lump. What I saw: the crushed sugar was gone in 2 minutes, and the whole lump took 8 minutes. Why: the bits had much more outside touching the water. My lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny air bags, so lots of air touches my blood.

activities.title: Feel Your Inside

materials.item: your own body and a quiet place to sit
a glass of water
optional: a simple stethoscope, or a tube of rolled-up paper to put against the chest and listen through

activities.safety: No special safety needed. Press gently.

schedule.what: Feel for your heart, lungs, stomach and skull, one at a time.

activities.record: Draw a quick outline of yourself. Put a dot where you felt each thing.
activities.context: This is a short activity to notice your organs from the outside, before learning about them. You feel your heartbeat, your breathing, a swallow and your skull.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged with a flat hand on the middle of the chest, eyes closed.
setup.caption: 1. Hand on chest. Feel for a beat.

setup.art: A child with both hands on the sides of the ribs, breathing in, the ribs lifting out.
setup.caption: 2. Hands on ribs. Breathe in deep.

setup.art: A child sipping water with one hand gently resting on the neck and the other just under the left ribs.
setup.caption: 3. Sip water. Follow it down.

setup.art: A child knocking gently on the top of the head with one knuckle.
setup.caption: 4. Knock gently on your head.

flow.do: 1. Sit together quietly. 2. Ask your child to put a flat hand on the middle of their chest and keep still.
flow.say: Put your hand flat on the middle of your chest. Be very still. What do you feel? Now move your hand a little to the left. Is it stronger?
flow.kid: Put your hand on your chest. Be very still. What do you feel? Move it a little left.

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: A thump.
It's stronger on the left.
Why does it never stop?

flow.context: This is the first step of Feel Your Inside, a short activity to notice your organs from the outside. Here you feel for your heart.

flow.do: Ask your child to put both hands on their ribs and breathe in slowly and deeply, then out.
flow.say: Hands on your ribs. Breathe in slowly, as much as you can. What happens to your hands? Now breathe out.
flow.kid: Hands on your ribs. Breathe in slowly. Do your hands move? Breathe out.
flow.parent: The ribs lift up and out as the lungs fill. A good wonder is 'What is inside that is getting bigger?'

flow.do: Ask your child to take a sip of water and feel it go down, with one hand on the throat.
flow.say: Take a sip. Swallow. Feel your throat move. Where do you think the water goes next?
flow.kid: Sip some water. Swallow. Feel your throat move. Where does the water go?

check.q: When you swallow water, where does it go?
options: Down the food pipe to the stomach
check.why: Swallowed food and drink go down the food pipe into the stomach, under your ribs on the left. A little flap closes the windpipe when you swallow, so water does not go into the lungs. That is why water 'going down the wrong way' makes you cough. Picking 'lungs' usually means thinking of the throat as one tube. It is really two tubes side by side.

flow.do: Ask your child to knock gently on the top of their head, then draw dots on a quick outline.
flow.say: Knock gently on your head. That hard part is your skull. What do you think is inside? Now draw yourself and put a dot for each thing you felt.
flow.kid: Knock gently on your head. That is your skull. What is inside? Draw yourself. Put a dot for each thing you felt.
flow.think: You felt your heart, your breath, your swallow and your skull. What do you think you could not feel at all?

activities.title: The Life-size Organ Map

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, as long as your child, or old newspapers taped together
a marker pen
coloured paper: pink, red, yellow and brown
safety scissors and glue

activities.safety: Use safety scissors. A grown-up helps with long cuts.

schedule.what: Trace your child, guess the organs, cut them to size, place them, then check and move them.

activities.record: Take a photo of the map before and after you check it. Keep the map for the project and the challenge.
activities.context: This is the life-size organ map. You draw round your child on big paper, cut out organs at the right size and put them where they really go, inside the outline of your own body.

setup.art: A child lying on a long sheet of paper while a grown-up traces round them with a marker.
setup.caption: 1. Lie down on the paper. A grown-up traces round you.

setup.art: A child's closed fist next to a red paper heart of the same size, and two hands next to a brain shape.
setup.caption: 2. Cut out organs using your own hands as a guide to size.

setup.art: A child kneeling over the life-size outline, placing paper lungs, heart, stomach and brain inside it.
setup.caption: 3. Put each organ where you think it goes.

setup.art: The finished organ map pinned on a wall, with the child pointing at the stomach under the left ribs.
setup.caption: 4. Check the places and move any that are wrong.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper on the floor. 2. Ask your child to lie on it with arms a little out. 3. Trace round them with a marker.
flow.say: Lie down on the paper. I'm going to draw round you. This is going to be a map of you, from the inside.
flow.kid: Lie on the paper. Keep still. A grown-up draws round you. This will be a map of your inside.
flow.context: This is the first step of the life-size organ map. You trace round your body, then add your organs at the right size.

flow.do: Before cutting anything, ask your child to draw with a pencil where they think the brain, heart, lungs and stomach go.
flow.say: Before we look anything up, draw where you think your organs are. Just a pencil shape. It's fine to guess.
flow.kid: Draw where you think your brain, heart, lungs and stomach are. Just guess. Use a pencil.
flow.parent: This is your child's first model. Do not correct it yet. Many children draw a small heart on the far left, small lungs and a stomach low behind the belly button.

flow.do: Cut out organs at these sizes, using your child's hands as a guide. Heart: the size of their closed fist, red. Brain: two fists side by side, pink. Each lung: a tall leaf shape as long as their hand and a half, pink. Make the left lung a bit narrower, with a dent. Stomach: a J shape about as big as their open hand, yellow. Intestines: a long brown strip, coiled.
flow.say: Your heart is about the size of your fist. Your brain is about two fists. Let's cut them out using your own hands to measure.
flow.kid: Make a fist. Your heart is this big. Cut a red heart this size. Your brain is two fists. Cut that too.
flow.parent: These sizes are rough guides. The lungs are bigger than most children expect. They fill most of the chest.

flow.do: Ask your child to place each organ on the map. Then read the body map card together and move any that are wrong.
flow.say: Put each organ where you think it goes. Now let's check with the card. Heart in the middle, tipped left. Lungs on both sides. Stomach under the ribs on the left. Brain in the head.
flow.kid: Put each organ on your map. Now check. Heart in the middle. Lungs on both sides. Stomach under the left ribs. Brain in the head.

check.q: On your organ map, where do the lungs go?
options: Two small circles near the shoulders
Filling most of the chest, one on each side of the heart
check.why: The lungs are big. They fill most of the chest, from just above the collarbones to low down inside the ribs, one on each side of the heart. Picking 'small circles' usually means picturing lungs like two balloons. They are more like two big spongy leaves. The belly holds the stomach and intestines.

flow.do: Glue the organs down. Compare the pencil guesses with where the organs are now.
flow.say: Look at your pencil guesses, and where the organs are now. What did you move? What surprised you?
flow.kid: Glue the organs down. Look at your pencil guesses. What did you move? What surprised you?

good: The lungs are so big.
The heart is in the middle.
The stomach is higher up.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer for the organ map sounds like this. What I think: my stomach is under my ribs on the left, not behind my belly button. What I saw: the body map card put it there, and I felt full there after lunch. Why: the food pipe goes down the chest and ends there.

activities.title: Kitchen Organ Weigh-in

materials.item: a kitchen scale. If you have none, use packets with the weight printed on them, like a 1-kilogram packet of atta and a 200-gram packet of dal.
things from the kitchen: a packet of atta, a mango or apple, a bottle of water, dal, onions
paper and pencil

activities.safety: Do not lift heavy bags. A grown-up handles anything breakable.

schedule.what: Find kitchen things that weigh about the same as a grown-up's heart, brain and lungs, and things that hold as much as a full stomach.

activities.record: Make a table: organ, what weighs the same, its weight in grams.
activities.context: This is a kitchen activity. You find foods that weigh about the same as a grown-up's organs, so you can feel how heavy each one is in your hands.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with a mango on it showing about 300 grams.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up's heart weighs about 300 grams. Find something that weighs the same.

setup.art: A packet of atta and a small onion on a scale showing about 1,300 grams.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up's brain weighs about 1,300 grams. Build it with kitchen things.

setup.art: A child holding a 1-litre water bottle in both hands.
setup.caption: 3. A full grown-up stomach holds about 1 litre. Hold a 1-litre bottle.

flow.do: Weigh things until you find something close to 300 grams. Let your child hold it.
flow.say: A grown-up's heart weighs about 300 grams. Let's find something that weighs the same. Hold it. Your heart is a bit lighter, because you are smaller.
flow.kid: A grown-up's heart is about 300 grams. Find something that weighs that much. Hold it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the kitchen organ weigh-in. You find kitchen things as heavy as a grown-up's heart, brain and lungs.

flow.do: Build up about 1,300 grams with a packet of atta and something small. Let your child hold it with two hands.
flow.say: A grown-up's brain weighs about 1,300 grams. That is one kilogram and three hundred grams. Hold it. This is what sits on top of your neck all day.
flow.kid: A grown-up's brain is about 1,300 grams. Put things on the scale until it says that. Hold it.

check.q: Which is heavier in a grown-up, the brain or the heart?
check.why: A grown-up's brain weighs about 1,300 grams. The heart weighs about 300 grams. So the brain is more than four times heavier. Picking 'the heart' often comes from how important and strong the heart feels. It is strong, but small.

flow.do: Let your child hold a 1-litre water bottle, then an empty bottle.
flow.say: When a grown-up's stomach is comfortably full, it holds about one litre, like this bottle. When it is empty, it is small, like a fist.
flow.kid: Hold the full bottle. A full stomach holds about this much. An empty one is small, like your fist.

flow.do: Make the table together: organ, kitchen match, weight in grams.
flow.say: Let's write it down. Which organ was heaviest? Which surprised you?
flow.kid: Write a table. Organ, kitchen thing, grams. Which was heaviest?
flow.parent: The two lungs together weigh about 1 kilogram in a grown-up, but they are mostly air and very light for their size. The liver, under the right ribs, is the heaviest organ inside, about 1,500 grams.

activities.title: The Body Council (act it out)

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper to make signs: BRAIN, HEART, LUNGS, STOMACH
soft toys or family members to play organs

activities.safety: Act in a clear space with nothing to trip on.

schedule.what: Act out four moments of a day with the brain, heart, lungs and stomach as characters.

activities.record: Draw one scene as a comic strip with four boxes.
activities.context: This is a drama game. Your child plays the brain, the Brain Mayor, and family members or toys play the heart, lungs and stomach. You act out how they work together in four moments of a day.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair wearing a paper sign saying BRAIN, with a parent holding a HEART sign and two soft toys with LUNGS and STOMACH signs.
setup.caption: 1. Make signs. The child is the Brain Mayor.

setup.art: The child pointing and giving orders while the parent with the HEART sign drums fast on a tin.
setup.caption: 2. Act out a moment. The brain sends messages.

setup.art: The child slumped sleepily while the STOMACH toy is wiggled and the HEART drums slowly.
setup.caption: 3. Change the moment. Watch how each organ changes.

flow.do: Make the four signs. Your child is the BRAIN, sitting on a chair. You are the HEART. Toys are LUNGS and STOMACH.
flow.say: You are the Brain Mayor. You get messages and send orders. I am the heart. I drum the beat. Teddy is the lungs. Dolly is the stomach.
flow.kid: You are the brain. You get messages and give orders. Who is the heart? Who are the lungs and stomach?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Body Council, a drama game where family members act as organs.

flow.do: Act out 'A dog barks suddenly'. The brain hears it and orders the heart to drum faster and the lungs to breathe faster. The stomach stops for a while.
flow.say: Woof! A big dog barks! Brain Mayor, what do you tell everyone?
flow.kid: A dog barks! You are the brain. What do you tell the heart and lungs?
flow.parent: A good brain says: 'Heart, beat faster! Lungs, breathe faster! Stomach, wait!' This is what really happens when we are scared. Blood moves away from the stomach to the leg muscles.

flow.do: Act out 'A big lunch' and then 'Falling asleep'.
flow.say: Now lunch is here. Brain, what do you tell the stomach? Now it is night. What happens to the heart drum?
flow.kid: Lunch time! What does the stomach do? Now it's night. Is the heart drum fast or slow?

check.q: When you fall asleep, what does the brain do?
options: It keeps the heart and breathing going, more slowly
It stops the heart until morning
check.why: The brain never switches off. While you sleep, it keeps you breathing and keeps your heart beating, just more slowly. It even sorts out the day's memories. Picking 'switches off' is a common idea, because we are not aware when we sleep. But the brain is busy all night.

flow.do: Swap roles. Then ask the team question.
flow.say: Let's swap. Now I am the brain. Here is a puzzle for the council: could the Brain Mayor work if the heart went on holiday?
flow.kid: Swap roles. Could the brain work if the heart stopped?

ask.q: Why can't the heart ever take a holiday?
good: The brain needs blood every second.
Every cell needs oxygen all the time.

activities.title: Same Plan, Different Animals

materials.item: the printed animal cards from this activity, or a library book of animal bodies
optional: a visit with a grown-up to a fish market or a fish being cleaned at home, for families who eat fish
paper and coloured pencils

activities.safety: At a fish market, stay with a grown-up and keep your hands away from knives.

schedule.what: Compare where the heart, breathing organs, stomach and brain are in a fish, a cow, an octopus and you.

activities.record: Draw yourself and one other animal side by side, with the four organs in each.
activities.context: This activity compares our organs with the organs of other animals. You find out which animals have the same plan as us, and which are very different.

setup.art: Four picture cards laid out: a child, a fish, a cow and an octopus, each with a see-through body showing organs.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the animal cards.

setup.art: A child pointing at the heart on the fish card and then on the child card.
setup.caption: 2. Find the heart, the breathing organ, the stomach and the brain in each.

setup.art: A child drawing a fish and a child side by side with matching coloured organs.
setup.caption: 3. Draw yourself and one animal side by side.

flow.do: Look at the fish card, or a real fish being cleaned if your family eats fish. Find its heart, stomach, brain and swim bladder.
flow.say: A fish has a brain in a bony box, a small heart low behind the gills, a stomach and a gut. It breathes with gills. It also has an air bag called a swim bladder. That air bag is a distant cousin of your lungs.
flow.kid: Find the fish's brain, heart and stomach. It breathes with gills. Its air bag is a cousin of your lungs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Plan, Different Animals. You compare a fish's organs with yours.
flow.parent: If your family does not eat fish, use the picture card only. The swim bladder and lungs come from the same ancient beginning in early fish.

flow.do: Look at the cow and the octopus cards. Count the stomach parts and the hearts.
flow.say: A cow's stomach has four parts. An octopus has three hearts. Most of its nerve cells are in its arms, not its head.
flow.kid: Count the cow's stomach parts. Count the octopus's hearts.

check.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
check.why: An octopus has three hearts. Two pump blood through its gills and one pumps blood round the body. Picking 'eight' is a clever guess, because octopuses have eight arms, and most of their nerve cells are in the arms. But the hearts are three.

flow.do: Talk about the sponge: an animal with no organs.
flow.say: A sponge is one of the oldest kinds of animal. It has no heart, no stomach and no brain. So how does it stay alive?
flow.kid: A sponge has no heart, no stomach and no brain. How is it alive?

ask.q: How does a sponge eat and breathe without organs?
good: Each cell does it by itself.
Water flows through it and every cell takes what it needs.

flow.do: Draw yourself and one animal side by side, using the same colour for the same organ in each.
flow.say: Draw yourself and one animal. Use red for both hearts and pink for both brains. What is the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Draw you and one animal. Same colour for the same organ. What is the same?
flow.think: Why do you think a fish and you have the same plan inside?

activities.title: One Breath, One Bite: trace the team

materials.item: your life-size organ map from the earlier activity
red, blue and yellow wool or string, and tape

schedule.what: Use coloured string on the organ map to trace a breath of air and a bite of food, and see where they meet.

activities.record: Leave the strings on the map. Write one sentence on each string saying what it carries.
activities.context: This activity uses coloured string on your life-size organ map to show how organs work together. A blue string follows air, a yellow string follows food and a red string follows blood.

setup.art: The life-size organ map on the floor with a blue string taped from the nose down to the lungs.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a blue string from the nose to the lungs, for air.

setup.art: A yellow string taped from the mouth down to the stomach and on into the coiled intestines.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a yellow string from the mouth to the stomach, for food.

setup.art: A red string looping from the heart to the lungs, the stomach, the brain and the toes.
setup.caption: 3. Tape a red string from the heart to every organ, for blood.

flow.do: Tape a blue string from the nose, down the windpipe, into both lungs.
flow.say: This blue string is a breath of air. It goes in at the nose, down the windpipe and into both lungs.
flow.kid: Tape a blue string from the nose to the lungs. This is air.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Breath, One Bite. You use your organ map to show air, food and blood moving between organs.

flow.do: Tape a yellow string from the mouth, down the food pipe, to the stomach, then into the intestines.
flow.say: This yellow string is a bite of food. Mouth, food pipe, stomach, then the long intestines.
flow.kid: Tape a yellow string from the mouth to the stomach. Then on to the intestines. This is food.

flow.do: Tape a red string from the heart to the lungs, then to the intestines, the brain and a toe. Bring it back to the heart.
flow.say: The red string is blood. The heart pumps it to the lungs to pick up oxygen. It picks up food near the intestines. Then it takes both to the brain and the toes.
flow.kid: Tape a red string from the heart. Take it to the lungs, gut, brain and a toe. This is blood.

check.q: On the organ map, which string touches the blue air string and the yellow food string?
check.why: Blood picks up oxygen from the lungs and food from the intestines, and carries both to every cell. So the red string meets both. Picking 'none' usually means picturing organs as separate. The blood is what links them.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to the brain and say what it needs from each string.
flow.say: Point to the brain. What does it need from the red string?
flow.kid: Point to the brain. What does it need from the blood?

ask.q: What does the brain get from the blood?
good: Oxygen from the lungs.
Food from the stomach and intestines.

projects.title: My Inside Book: a lift-the-flap book

materials.item: 4 sheets of thick paper or card
coloured pencils or crayons
safety scissors, glue and a stapler

projects.safety: A grown-up uses the stapler. Use safety scissors.

schedule.what: Draw the cover: a child in a shirt. Cut the shirt into a flap that lifts up. Draw the four organs underneath.
Make one page each for the heart, lungs, stomach and brain: where it is, what it does and one amazing fact.
Staple the book together. Read it to someone younger, and ask them to point to their own organs.

projects.record: The finished book, and the name of the person you read it to.
projects.context: In this 3-day project, you make a lift-the-flap book about the organs inside you. Then you teach someone younger with it.

setup.art: A drawing of a child in a striped shirt, with the shirt cut as a flap and lifted to show a heart, lungs and stomach underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a child. Make the shirt a flap that lifts.

setup.art: Four book pages fanned out, each with a big drawing of one organ and three short lines of writing.
setup.caption: 2. Make one page for each organ.

setup.art: An older child reading the flap book to a younger child who is pointing at their own chest.
setup.caption: 3. Read it to someone younger.

flow.do: 1. On the cover, draw a child in a shirt. 2. Cut round three sides of the shirt so it lifts like a door. 3. Glue a second sheet behind and draw the organs in the right places under the flap.
flow.say: Under the shirt, draw what is really there. Brain in the head, lungs and heart in the chest, stomach under the left ribs.
flow.kid: Draw a child in a shirt. Cut the shirt so it opens. Draw the organs underneath, in the right places.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the My Inside Book project, a lift-the-flap book about your organs.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow for the organ pages.
flow.do: Make four pages. On each, draw one organ and write three lines: 'I live…', 'My job is…', 'Amazing fact…'.
flow.say: For each organ, write where it lives, what it does and one amazing fact.
flow.kid: One page for each organ. Write where it lives. Write its job. Write one amazing fact.

check.q: Which is a true amazing fact for your heart page?
options: The heart is on the far left of the chest
The heart can start a beat by itself, without the brain
check.why: The heart has its own tiny timekeeper that starts each beat. The brain only speeds it up or slows it down. The heart sits in the middle of the chest, tipped left, not far left. And thinking happens in the brain.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow to finish and share the book.
flow.do: 1. Staple the pages together behind the cover. 2. Read the book to a younger child or a grandparent. 3. Ask them to point to their own organs.
flow.say: Now you are the teacher. Read your book and ask them to point to their own heart and stomach.
flow.kid: Staple your book. Read it to someone. Ask them to point to their own heart and stomach.

ask.q: What did your listener find most surprising?
good: That the stomach is under the ribs.
That the brain is so heavy.
That an octopus has three hearts.

challenges.title: Helmet for an Egg Brain
challenges.problem: Design a helmet for a raw egg, so it can fall from the height of a table onto the floor without cracking.
constraints: You can only use things from home: paper, cloth, cotton, a plastic cup, rubber bands, tape.
The helmet must fit in two hands.
The egg must be easy to take out and check.
materials: raw eggs. No eggs at home? Use a very ripe tomato, and look for splits and soft squashed spots.
paper, cotton wool, cloth, a plastic cup, rubber bands and tape
a tray or newspaper on the floor
general: Wrap the egg in something soft, like cotton wool or cloth, so it is cushioned.
Put it in a hard cup on the outside, like a skull.
Make sure the egg cannot rattle around inside.
creative: Put the egg in a small bag of water inside the cup, like the liquid around your brain.
Look at a cricket or cycling helmet. It has a hard outside and soft foam inside. Copy the idea.
Add a paper parachute so the helmet lands more slowly.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own helmet. Draw it, build it and test it. Then make it better.
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a helmet that protects a raw egg in a fall, the way your skull and its liquid protect your brain.

setup.art: A table covered with cotton wool, a plastic cup, cloth, rubber bands and a raw egg.
setup.caption: 1. Collect soft and hard things.

setup.art: A child wrapping an egg in cotton wool and pushing it into a plastic cup.
setup.caption: 2. Build a helmet round the egg.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the helmet at table height above a tray on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Drop it from table height. Check the egg.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Remind your child of the egg in the jar test.
flow.say: Your skull is hard on the outside. Inside, your brain is cushioned by liquid. How could we copy that for an egg?
flow.kid: Your skull is hard outside. Liquid cushions your brain inside. How can you copy that?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Helmet for an Egg Brain challenge. You design a helmet to protect an egg in a fall.

flow.do: Your child draws a design, then builds it from things at home.
flow.say: Draw your helmet first. What is hard on the outside? What is soft inside?
flow.kid: Draw your helmet. Hard outside, soft inside. Then build it.

flow.do: Over a tray, a grown-up drops the helmet from table height. Open it and check the egg.
flow.say: Three, two, one, drop! Let's open it carefully. Is the egg whole?
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up. Drop it from the table over a tray. Open it. Is the egg whole?

check.q: Which helmet design is most like your real head?
options: A hard cup with something soft or watery inside
check.why: Your head has a hard skull outside, and a cushion of liquid and soft layers inside. Both together protect the brain best. A hard cup alone lets the egg bang on the inside. Soft cotton alone squashes in a hard fall.

flow.do: Improve the design and test once more.
flow.say: What would make it better? Change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Change one thing to make it better. Test again.
flow.think: Why do people wear helmets on scooters, even though they already have a skull?

challenges.title: Pack the Chest
challenges.problem: Fit a model heart and two model lungs inside a shallow box lid, so they fill the space without squashing each other.
constraints: Use playdough or atta dough for the organs.
Use the lid of a shoe box or a mithai box as the chest. It is shallow, so the model is flat.
The heart must be as wide as your fist, and the lungs must fill the rest.
materials: playdough, or dough made from about 2 cups of atta, in two colours (add a little haldi to one half)
the lid of a shoe box or a mithai box
paper strips for ribs, and tape
general: Make the heart first, as wide as your fist and about one finger thick, and put it in the middle.
Mould the lungs around it, one on each side.
Leave a dent in the left lung so the heart fits.
creative: Make the lungs fluffy by pressing in lots of tiny holes with a pencil tip, like tiny air bags.
Tape paper strips over the box as ribs, with small gaps between them.
Push in a straw for the windpipe and split it into two.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own chest model. What else could you add, like a dome-shaped diaphragm at the bottom?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You fit a model heart and two lungs into a box, to see why your left lung is smaller and how your ribs guard them.

setup.art: A shoe box lid, two colours of dough and a child's fist next to a flat red dough heart.
setup.caption: 1. Make a flat heart as wide as your fist.

setup.art: Two pink dough lungs moulded around the red heart inside the box, the left one with a dent.
setup.caption: 2. Mould the lungs around the heart.

setup.art: Paper strips taped across the top of the box like ribs, with the organs visible between them.
setup.caption: 3. Tape paper ribs over the top.

flow.do: Make a dough heart as wide as your child's fist and about one finger thick. Put it in the middle of the lid, tipped a little to the left.
flow.say: Your heart is about as big as your fist. Put it in the middle of the chest, tipped a little left.
flow.kid: Make a flat heart as wide as your fist. Put it in the middle, tipped left.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pack the Chest challenge. You fit a heart and two lungs into a model chest.

flow.do: Press the two lungs flat, about one finger thick, around the heart until the lid is full.
flow.say: Now fill all the rest of the space with lungs. What do you have to do to the left lung?
flow.kid: Fill the rest of the lid with two flat lungs. What happens to the left lung?

check.q: Why is your left lung a little smaller than your right lung?
options: It leaves room for the heart
It holds less air because it is lazy
check.why: The heart is tipped to the left, so the left lung has a dent to make room for it. That is why the left lung is a little smaller. Organs are not 'lazy'. Their shapes fit together like puzzle pieces.

flow.do: Tape paper strips across the top as ribs.
flow.say: Now add the ribs, like the bars of a cage. Why leave gaps between them?
flow.kid: Tape paper ribs over the top. Leave gaps. Why?
flow.parent: Real ribs have muscles between them, and they swing up and out when you breathe in. A solid box would not let the lungs grow.

flow.do: Show the model to someone and explain it.
flow.say: Tell someone what each part is, and why the left lung has a dent.
flow.kid: Show your model. Explain each part.
flow.think: What would happen if the ribs were one solid sheet of bone?

opts: A body part with a special job
quiz.why: An organ is a body part with a special job, made of many cells. Picking 'only a bone' mixes up organs with the skeleton.

opts: In the middle of the chest, tipped a little left
quiz.why: The heart is in the middle of the chest, tipped left. Picking 'far left' comes from feeling the beat most there.

opts: Under the ribs on the left
In the middle of the chest
quiz.why: The stomach is under the ribs on the left. The belly below the belly button is mostly intestines.

opts: Two small balls near the neck
Filling most of the chest, on both sides of the heart
quiz.why: The lungs are big. They fill most of the chest. Picking 'small balls' is common, because we picture lungs like balloons.
The heart pumps blood. Picking 'thinks' is the old idea of Aristotle and the ancient Egyptians.

opts: Take oxygen into the blood and let out carbon dioxide
quiz.why: The lungs swap gases with the blood. Picking 'pump blood' mixes up the lungs with the heart.

opts: Holds food and churns it with strong juices
quiz.why: The stomach holds, churns and breaks down food. Remember the squish bag test.

opts: Sends and receives messages, and lets us think, feel, remember and move
quiz.why: The brain does all of these, and also runs breathing and heartbeat speed without us noticing. Picking 'only schoolwork' is too small a picture.

quiz.p: Which bones protect the heart and lungs?
quiz.why: The ribs make a cage around the chest. The skull protects the brain.

quiz.p: In the egg in the jar test, what did the water stand for?
opts: The liquid that cushions the brain
quiz.why: The water around the egg stood for the clear liquid around the brain. The jar stood for the skull.

opts: The brain tells the heart and lungs to work faster
The stomach takes over from the heart
quiz.why: Organs work as a team. The brain speeds up the heart and breathing so the muscles get more oxygen.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: How the brain makes a thought or a feeling
quiz.why: Where organs are and what they do is well known. How a brain makes the feeling of being you is one of the biggest open questions in science.

quiz.p: A sponge has no organs. How does it live?
opts: Water flows through it, and its cells take oxygen and food from the water
quiz.why: Organs are teams of cells sharing out jobs. A sponge has no organs. Its cells take oxygen and food straight from the water flowing through it.

quiz.p: How many hearts does an octopus have?
quiz.why: Three: two for the gills and one for the body. Picking 'eight' guesses one per arm.

applications: Doctors use a stethoscope to listen to the heart and lungs through the chest.
X-rays show bones and swallowed objects, like coins and marbles, inside the body.
Ultrasound scans show a beating heart and a baby growing inside the mother.
MRI scanners take pictures of the brain without any cutting.
Cricket, cycling and scooter helmets protect the skull and the brain inside it.
Heart transplants give a new heart to a person whose own heart is failing. The first one in India was done in Delhi in 1994.
Organ donation lets one person's organs save several other lives after they die.
Machines called ventilators help people breathe when their lungs are very ill.
Pacemakers are small devices that keep a heartbeat steady when the heart's own timekeeper goes wrong.
Doctors look inside the stomach with a thin tube that has a tiny camera on the end.
Mini-organs grown in labs help scientists test new medicines.
Seat belts and airbags in cars protect the chest and head in a crash.
First aid teaches people how to help someone who is choking, by clearing the windpipe.
Animal doctors use the same knowledge to treat cows, dogs and cats, which have most of the same organs as us.

open_questions.q: How does the brain make a thought, a dream or the feeling of being you?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see which parts of the brain are busy, but not how busy nerve cells turn into a feeling. This is one of the biggest puzzles in science.

open_questions.q: Why do we sleep, and what is the brain doing all night?
open_questions.why_open: Sleep helps memory and clears waste from the brain. But scientists still argue about its main job.

open_questions.q: How much do the germs in our gut change how we feel?
open_questions.why_open: Tests in mice show gut germs can change behaviour. Tests in people are new, and the results are mixed.

open_questions.q: Can we grow a whole new heart, lung or stomach from a person's own cells?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can grow tiny mini-organs. Nobody has yet grown a full-sized working one for a person.

open_questions.q: How many organs does a body have?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on what you count as an organ. Scientists still argue about new ones, like the interstitium.

open_questions.q: Do animals with very different brains, like octopuses, feel things the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: An octopus solves puzzles and plays. But its brain is built very differently, and we cannot ask it what it feels.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does the heart's own timekeeper stay so steady for a whole life?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand a lot about it. But how it stays steady for billions of beats, and why it sometimes goes wrong, is still being studied.

jokes.j: Why did the heart get a medal?

jokes.j: What did the left lung say to the right lung?
jokes.a: Take a deep breath. We're in this together.

jokes.j: Why was the stomach so good at school?
jokes.a: It could really digest the lessons.

jokes.j: Why did the brain go to the party?
jokes.a: It wanted to make some new connections.

jokes.j: What do you call a heart that loves music?
jokes.a: A beat box.

jokes.j: Why did the skull not go to the dance?
jokes.a: It had no body to go with.

jokes.j: What is a stomach's favourite exercise?
jokes.a: Crunches.

jokes.j: Why are lungs never lonely?

maths.problem: In the kitchen weigh-in, a grown-up's brain weighed about 1,300 grams and a grown-up's heart about 300 grams. How much heavier is the brain?
maths.explain: The brain is about 1,300 grams. The heart is about 300 grams. 1,300 take away 300 is 1,000. So the brain is 1,000 grams, or 1 kilogram, heavier.
maths.why_maths: Holding things tells us roughly which is heavier. Taking one weight from the other tells us exactly how much heavier.
maths.context: This is about the kitchen organ weigh-in, where you found kitchen things that weigh the same as a grown-up's organs.

chart.title: About how much a grown-up's organs weigh

maths.problem: A grown-up's heart beats about 70 times in one minute. How many times does it beat in 10 minutes?
maths.explain: In one minute it beats about 70 times. In 10 minutes, that is 10 groups of 70. 70 times 10 is 700. So about 700 beats in 10 minutes.
maths.why_maths: You felt your heartbeat with your hand. Multiplying helps us see how many beats add up, even when we cannot count them all.
maths.context: This is about Feel Your Inside, where you put a hand on your chest to feel your heart beating.

maths.problem: A grown-up's full stomach holds about 1 litre. A steel tumbler holds about 250 millilitres. How many tumblers of food would fill the stomach?
maths.explain: 1 litre is 1,000 millilitres. 250 plus 250 plus 250 plus 250 is 1,000. So 4 tumblers fill 1 litre.
maths.why_maths: A litre is hard to picture. Counting tumblers makes the size of a full stomach easy to see.
maths.context: This is about the kitchen organ weigh-in, where you held a 1-litre bottle to feel how much a full stomach holds.

maths.problem: Say that in the lump or bits test, the whole lump of mishri took 8 minutes to disappear and the crushed lump took 2 minutes. How many times as long did the whole lump take?
maths.explain: The whole lump took 8 minutes. The crushed lump took 2 minutes. 8 divided by 2 is 4. You can check: 2 plus 2 plus 2 plus 2 is 8. So the whole lump took 4 times as long.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells us 'how many times as long', which shows how much breaking sugar into small bits speeds it up.
maths.context: This is about the lump or bits test, where you timed a whole lump and a crushed lump of mishri disappearing into water.

maths.problem: On the life-size organ map, the heart was 1 fist wide and the brain was 2 fists wide. If one fist is 7 centimetres, how wide was the brain?
maths.explain: The brain was 2 fists wide. Each fist is 7 centimetres. 7 plus 7 is 14. So the brain was about 14 centimetres wide.
maths.why_maths: Fists are handy for guessing sizes. Changing fists into centimetres lets us compare with a ruler and with other people.
maths.context: This is about the life-size organ map, where you cut out organs using your own fist to measure their size.

roots.context: We have been learning where the heart, lungs, stomach and brain are, and what they do. Now we ask what these organs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Shake a raw egg or a ripe banana piece in an empty jar, and it cracks or squashes. In a jar filled to the top with water, it stays whole. Your brain floats in liquid inside your skull, and that liquid protects it the same way. Hard bone alone would not keep a soft brain safe.
deep_truth.habit: We often think that keeping something safe means making it hard, like armour. But a soft thing inside a hard case can still crash into the walls and break. Your body keeps its softest organ safe with liquid as well as bone.
deep_truth.evidence: In the egg in the jar test, the egg in the empty jar cracked first, and the egg in the jar full of water stayed whole. Inside your skull, your brain floats in a clear liquid in the same way. A cricket helmet copies the idea, with a hard shell outside and soft foam inside.

three.who_am_i: You are a team of organs, from your brain to your stomach, and every one of them is made of living cells.
three.what_is_life: A living body keeps going because its organs pass blood, food, air and messages to each other all the time.
three.what_is_this_world: A fish, a cow and you each have a brain in a skull, a heart and a gut, because all animals with backbones share one ancestor.

roots.thread: Long ago, every living thing was a single cell that did every job by itself. Over a very long time, some cells began to live together as one body and share out the work. Some became heart cells that squeeze, some became lung cells that swap gases, and some became nerve cells that carry messages. The jobs one cell once did alone are now shared among many organs. Those many organs still keep one body alive together.

teachings.teaching: The senses and breath once argued about which of them was the greatest. Speech, sight, hearing and mind each left the body in turn, and the body carried on. When breath, prana, began to leave, all the others were pulled up with it. They agreed breath was the one they all depended on.
teachings.link: In this unit, the brain is badly hurt within minutes if the heart's blood stops, and every organ needs the oxygen your lungs bring in. The old story also puts breath at the centre of the body.

teachings.source: Saint Paul, First Letter to the Corinthians 12:12–26
teachings.teaching: The body is one, though it has many parts. The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I don't need you.' If one part suffers, every part suffers with it.
teachings.link: Scientists see the same thing. When the heart stops, the brain is hurt within minutes. When the lungs struggle, every organ struggles.

teachings.teaching: A newborn baby is soft and bendy, and a dead body is hard and stiff. Green plants bend, and dry dead ones snap. So the hard and stiff go with death, and the soft and bending go with life.
teachings.link: Your brain is one of the softest parts of you. In the egg test, the soft water around the egg protected it better than the hard jar alone.

science.text: All animals with backbones share an ancient ancestor. That is why a fish and a child have a brain in a skull, a heart in front and a gut below, and why lungs and swim bladders began as one thing.
Nobody knows how a brain makes the feeling of being someone. Scientists and philosophers call this the hard problem.

other_view.who: Most brain scientists, and the old Indian Charvaka school
other_view.view: You are your brain and body, and nothing more. When the body stops, the self stops too. The teamwork of organs is amazing, but nothing beyond the body is needed to explain it. That is an honest view, and many thoughtful people hold it.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,350 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught that the heart does our thinking and feeling. He thought the brain was there to cool the blood. Many people agreed, because the heart races when we are scared or excited. Some Greek doctors disagreed. In Alexandria, about 2,300 years ago, Herophilus cut open human bodies and traced the nerves back to the brain. About 1,850 years ago, the Greek doctor Galen, working in Rome, tested the idea in front of an audience. He cut two thin nerves in the neck of a squealing pig. The pig went silent, though its heart kept beating and it kept breathing. Galen showed that these nerves came from the brain, not the heart. So the brain, he said, controls the voice. He also cut the spinal cord of animals at different places, and showed which parts of the body could no longer move. Today we have even stronger proof. People living with a machine that pumps their blood still think, laugh and remember.
how_we_found_out.when: About 350 BCE (Aristotle), about 300 BCE (Herophilus) and about 160 CE (Galen's pig experiment)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle taught that the heart does the thinking and the brain only cools the blood. Galen cut the nerves that control a pig's voice, and showed that they come from the brain. The pig fell silent while its heart kept beating.
